idiom_name: readonly T[] view over a #private field
implementation_notes: TypeScript gives a type-level read-only view but no runtime enforcement: publish `get courses(): readonly Course[]` (ReadonlyArray<Course>) so the compiler rejects push/splice/index assignment - the handbook says ReadonlyArray is 'mainly a tool we can use for intent' and notes there is no ReadonlyArray constructor - and pair it with a runtime guard, either a `#courses` private field (ES2022, enforced by the engine) or a getter that returns `[...this.#courses]`. A TypeScript `private courses: Course[]` alone is erased at compile time, so JavaScript callers (or a cast) can still reach the array; that is why the field should be `#`-private, not merely `private`. Mutators addCourse/removeCourse own validation, and `Object.freeze` on the returned copy gives a snapshot immutable even from untyped callers.
pitfalls: `readonly` and `private` are erased at runtime: JavaScript callers, `as any` casts or a proxy can still mutate the array - keep a #private field or return a copy when the boundary is not types-only.
`readonly T[]` is not assignable back to `T[]`, so consumers that need a mutable working copy must explicitly slice/spread it - a deliberate, documented cost.
A getter with no setter is inferred read-only in emitted .d.ts; adding a setter later silently relaxes the contract, so keep mutators as separate methods.
Structural typing means an object literal with a mutable array still satisfies an interface declaring `readonly T[]`: the guarantee is per-reference, not per-value.
